title: Ownership and Deletion Mismatch
platform_conditions: C++11 and later on any conforming toolchain; smart-pointer adoption depends on the codebase's C++ standard baseline
security_mechanism: `new T[]` must be released with delete[] because the array form stores a count and runs the destructor loop; plain delete on an array pointer runs one destructor and hands a differently-shaped block to the allocator, corrupting the heap. Naked new/delete make ownership implicit, so two code paths that both 'own' the same pointer produce a double free, and a path that forgets its delete leaks until the resource (a lock file, a credential handle) is exhausted. shared_ptr adds its own trap: two shared_ptr instances constructed from the same raw pointer hold two independent control blocks, destroying the object twice when each hits zero.

source_sink_clues.source: Object lifetimes steered by request flow: early returns, error paths, and re-handoff of buffers between modules, any of which can free or re-take ownership while another path still holds the pointer.
source_sink_clues.sink: delete applied to a new[] pointer; two owners freeing one raw pointer; shared_ptr constructed from a raw pointer already owned elsewhere

tracking_guards: Check that allocation goes through make_unique/make_shared (never naked new held in raw pointers), that array allocations use unique_ptr<T[]> or std::vector, and that no raw pointer that already has an owner is passed to a smart-pointer constructor or deleted a second time.
not_candidate_when: The allocation is owned exclusively by a smart pointer and no raw alias is ever deleted, the raw pointer is non-owning (observer) by documented convention and its owner provably outlives all users, or the array is a compile-time constant replaced by std::array/vector.
public_references: CWE-404: Improper Resource Shutdown or Release — https://cwe.mitre.org/data/definitions/404.html
C++ Core Guidelines: R resource-management rules — https://isocpp.github.io/CppCoreGuidelines/CppCoreGuidelines
